title: Deck of Cards
description: Build a 52-card deck as a class — constructor populates rank+suit strings, draw() pops the top, reset() rebuilds. The shape every card-game interview problem starts from.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the API and the card representation.
sections.say:
"Let me make sure I have this right: I need a Deck class with three operations — a constructor that builds a fresh 52-card deck, `size()` returning how many cards are left, `draw()` returning one card off the top, and `reset()` rebuilding the deck. The card itself can be just a string like 'Kc' (king of clubs) — no need for a per-card class."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Does the constructor build a shuffled deck or a deterministic one? (For this version: deterministic — shuffle is a separate concern.)
• Should `draw()` on an empty deck throw, or return undefined?
• Cards 2-10 — write '10' as a two-char token, or 'T'? (Both work; '10' is more natural to read.)
• Suits as letters (s/h/d/c) or unicode glyphs (♠♥♦♣)? (Letters are safer for terminal output; glyphs look nicer.)
sections.why: The 'deterministic vs shuffled' question is the big one. Shuffle is a totally separate algorithm (Fisher-Yates) with its own bugs (off-by-one indexing, wrong RNG range, not in-place); if the prompt didn't ask for shuffle, building it in unprompted wastes interview time AND adds bug surface. The 10-vs-T question signals you've thought about card-display formats — most poker libraries use 'T' so every card is one char, but interviews usually accept '10'. Asking just demonstrates awareness.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious shapes and pick the one that scales.
sections.say:
"There are a few ways to build the 52 cards. The dumb one is to write all 52 string literals in an array — works, but it's 52 lines of boilerplate and you'll typo at least one. The next-step-up is two nested loops — outer over suits, inner over ranks — pushing `rank + suit` to a cards array. Thirteen ranks times four suits, fifty-two pushes, no typos possible.

For the actual ops: I want `draw()` to be O(1). That means `pop()` off the end of the array, not `shift()` from the front — `shift` reindexes the whole array, which is O(n). The 'top' of the deck is conceptually the end of the array; it's a stack.

And `reset()` shouldn't duplicate the build logic in the constructor — I'll put the build inside `reset()` and have the constructor just call `reset()`. One source of truth."
sections.why: The nested-loop-build is the load-bearing technique here — it's what generalizes from this problem to any 'enumerate the Cartesian product of two small finite sets' problem (permutations of dice, all combinations of toppings, all directions × magnitudes for a chess piece). The pop-vs-shift call is the O(1)-vs-O(n) tradeoff that comes up constantly with arrays-as-stacks in JS; mentioning it shows you know which Array methods reindex and which don't. The constructor-delegates-to-reset move is the single-source-of-truth refactor that prevents the build logic from drifting between two places.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What data structure, and what invariants does it enforce?
sections.say:
"The data structure is an array of strings, used as a stack — push to build, pop to draw. The invariants: (1) the array contains each card exactly once after a fresh reset; (2) draw() removes from the end so order matches what was pushed last; (3) reset() restores the array to a known starting state so the deck is reusable across rounds.

The deterministic build order matters because of (3): if reset doesn't produce a predictable starting state, tests and game logic can't make assertions like 'after reset, the top is K of clubs'. Pushing in (suit-major, rank-minor) order means clubs come last, K is the last rank — so K of clubs ends up on top after a fresh deck. That's the canonical starting state for this build.

The reason to put the rebuild logic in reset() rather than inline in the constructor: any game using this deck will hit `reset()` between hands. If the constructor does the work and reset doesn't, the second hand starts with a partially-drawn deck."
sections.why: Naming the deterministic-start-state invariant is the bit interviewers grade on. 'Use an array' alone is trivia; 'array of strings with this specific build order so reset is testable and idempotent' is the design. The constructor-delegates-to-reset move is the same DRY idea that powers OOP-style initializers in larger classes — extract the 'set me to initial state' logic into a method, call it from the constructor, and you've got a reusable reset for free. That pattern shows up everywhere from React class component setState to database fixture reset.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few operation sequences to confirm the build order and the reset behavior.
sections.intro: "Let me trace three sequences. Each shows the deck's top card, size, and the collected results from every op. Because the build is deterministic (suit order spades→hearts→diamonds→clubs, rank order A→2→...→K), the very first draw is always K of clubs. The third example confirms that reset truly restores the top."

examples.input: size, draw, draw, draw, size, reset, size
examples.note: Canonical case — first three draws come off the top of clubs in descending rank (K, Q, J) because clubs is the last suit pushed and ranks are pushed A→K within each suit.
examples.trace:
init cards = [...52 cards built suit-major...], top='Kc'
size     → 52                    results=[52]
draw     → pop 'Kc' → cards now 51, top='Qc'   results=[52,'Kc']
draw     → pop 'Qc' → cards now 50, top='Jc'   results=[52,'Kc','Qc']
draw     → pop 'Jc' → cards now 49, top='10c'  results=[52,'Kc','Qc','Jc']
size     → 49                    results=[52,'Kc','Qc','Jc',49]
reset    → rebuild 52 cards, top='Kc' again
size     → 52                    results=[52,'Kc','Qc','Jc',49,52]
return [52,'Kc','Qc','Jc',49,52]

examples.input: draw, draw, draw, draw, draw, size
examples.note: Five consecutive draws strip the top of the clubs suit. After five draws, size is 52-5=47, top would be 8c.
examples.trace:
init cards has 52 entries, top='Kc'
draw     → 'Kc' → size 51, top='Qc'    results=['Kc']
draw     → 'Qc' → size 50, top='Jc'    results=['Kc','Qc']
draw     → 'Jc' → size 49, top='10c'   results=['Kc','Qc','Jc']
draw     → '10c' → size 48, top='9c'   results=['Kc','Qc','Jc','10c']
draw     → '9c' → size 47, top='8c'    results=['Kc','Qc','Jc','10c','9c']
size     → 47                          results=['Kc','Qc','Jc','10c','9c',47]
return ['Kc','Qc','Jc','10c','9c',47]

examples.note: Reset restores the deck to its starting state — the second draw returns Kc again because reset rebuilt the array from scratch.
examples.trace:
init cards has 52, top='Kc'
size     → 52                    results=[52]
draw     → 'Kc' → size 51, top='Qc'   results=[52,'Kc']
reset    → rebuild → size 52, top='Kc'
draw     → 'Kc' → size 51, top='Qc'   results=[52,'Kc','Kc']
return [52,'Kc','Kc']

sections.why: The first trace surfaces the off-by-one bug that bites every candidate who reverses the build order — if you loop ranks outer and suits inner, you'd get A♠, A♥, A♦, A♣, 2♠... and the top of the deck would be K of clubs only if you matched the prompt's iteration order. Reading the build order off the trace is the sanity check. The third trace is the load-bearing test for reset() — it has to actually rebuild, not just reset a cursor; otherwise the second draw would return 'Qc', not 'Kc'.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• Draw on empty deck → `pop()` on `[]` returns undefined. The prompt usually says assume non-empty draws; I'd flag that we'd return undefined silently rather than throw. A defensive version could throw, but undefined matches JS array semantics.
• Draw 52 times in a row → fine, just empties the array. The 53rd draw is the empty case above.
• Reset between hands → rebuilds the full 52, including any cards held by players. In a real card game I'd have a `discard()` method that returns cards to the deck WITHOUT rebuilding, but that's a different problem; reset is the nuclear option.
• Constructor called twice (`new Deck()` then `new Deck()`) → each is a fresh instance with its own cards array. No shared state. ✓
• Two-char rank '10' — make sure your build doesn't accidentally output '10c' as three chars when other ranks are two — it does, and that's correct, but parsers downstream need to handle variable-length rank tokens.
• Unicode suits (♠♥♦♣) — fine for display, but each is 1 codepoint and 1 UTF-16 unit, so length-based parsing still works. Emoji card suits would be more complex.
• Shuffle is a separate concern → reset doesn't shuffle. If the interviewer wants shuffled, that's a Fisher-Yates pass added after reset(), in-place."
sections.why: The 'discard vs reset' distinction is the senior-engineer flag — it shows you've thought about how this Deck class would slot into a real card game (poker hand → discard pile → reshuffle when draw pile is empty) versus an interview demo. Mentioning Fisher-Yates by name without launching into it shows you know the standard shuffle algorithm exists and could be added in 5 lines, without derailing the current scope. The variable-length rank token bullet is the tiny detail that bites parsers — interviewers love when candidates catch their own data-format inconsistencies.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity and place this design?
sections.say:
"Time: constructor and reset() are O(52) — fifty-two pushes, technically O(n) in the deck size but n is a constant 52, so it's effectively O(1). draw() and size() are both O(1) — pop is constant time, length is a property access. No method touches more than one cell per call (except the build).

Space: O(52) per Deck instance — the cards array. Each card is a 2- or 3-character string, so the whole deck is a few hundred bytes. Trivial.

The 'build via nested loop over enumerated dimensions' pattern is everywhere: building a chess board (8 ranks × 8 files), enumerating all hours in a week (7 days × 24 hours), generating all pixel coordinates of an image (height × width). Anywhere you have a small finite Cartesian product, two nested for-loops with a single push to a flat array is the cleanest expression.

The 'class with idempotent reset()' pattern shows up in game state machines, test fixtures, and any object that needs to be 'restored to initial state' without throwing it away and re-allocating. Calling reset from the constructor is the same DRY move that powers React's componentWillMount / componentDidMount split — initialization logic lives in one place.

If I wanted to extend this to multiple decks (a six-deck blackjack shoe), I'd loop the build six times inside reset() — same pattern, just with a `deckCount` parameter. The structure scales without changing shape."
sections.why: The nested-loop-enumeration generalization is the wrap-up move — most candidates can build the deck, but few articulate WHY the technique is reusable. The reset-as-pattern callout (game state machines, test fixtures) shows you see the design at a higher level than 'cards' — that's how the same shape powers a Minesweeper board reset, a Snake game restart, and a test setup hook. The six-deck-shoe extension is a tiny throwaway that demonstrates the design parameterizes cleanly — which is what scaling means in an interview answer.

walkthrough.intro: Step through a sequence of Deck operations. Each example is an op list — `size`, `draw`, `reset`. The canonical deck is deterministic (no shuffle); after `reset()` the top of the deck is K of clubs because clubs is the last suit pushed. The trace collects every size/draw result into a `results` array.

examples.label: size→52; draw → Kc; reset; draw → Kc (top restored)

trace: for (const s of SUITS) for (const r of RANKS) cards.push(r + s);

yield { line: 3, label: 'new Deck() → reset() builds 52 cards. top=' + cards[cards.length - 1] + ' (last pushed, drawn first)', state: { ops, top: cards[cards.length - 1], bottom: cards[0], size: cards.length, results: [] } };
yield { line: 11, label: 'op#' + k + ': size() = ' + cards.length, state: { ops, top: cards[cards.length - 1] || null, size: cards.length, results: [...results], op: o.op } };

yield { line: 12, label: 'op#' + k + ': draw() pops top → ' + v + ' (size now ' + cards.length + ')', state: { ops, top: cards[cards.length - 1] || null, size: cards.length, results: [...results], op: o.op } };
yield { line: 5, label: 'op#' + k + ': reset() — rebuild 52 cards', state: { ops, top: cards[cards.length - 1] || null, size: cards.length, results: [...results], op: o.op } };
yield { line: 9, label: 'rebuilt — size=' + cards.length + ', top=' + cards[cards.length - 1], state: { ops, top: cards[cards.length - 1], size: cards.length, results: [...results], op: o.op } };
yield { line: 13, label: 'all ops processed — results=' + JSON.stringify(results), state: { ops, size: cards.length, results: [...results], returns: JSON.stringify(results) } };

reference.approach: Nested rank×suit build, draw from the tail
notes: Card representation as `rank+suit` strings keeps state simple — no per-card class needed.
Use array.pop() so draw is O(1). `shift()` from the front would be O(n).
`reset()` is the single source of truth; the constructor just delegates to it.
Time O(1) per draw/size, O(52) per reset. Space O(52) per deck.

questions.q: Why use `pop()` instead of `shift()` for draw()?
options: shift() returns the array's new length; pop() returns the removed element
pop is O(1); shift is O(n) because it reindexes
shift() leaves a hole at index 0 (a sparse array), polluting future iteration
pop() removes from the head of the deck where new cards were just pushed
questions.explain: `shift()` has to reindex every remaining element down one slot, so dealing a whole deck would be O(n²). Treating the END of the array as the top of the deck makes each draw a single length decrement — and since the deck is shuffled anyway, which end is "the top" is arbitrary.

questions.q: How many cards does the constructor build?
questions.explain: The nested loop pairs each of 4 suits with each of 13 ranks — 4 × 13 = 52. The 54 option is the deck WITH jokers, which this build deliberately omits.

questions.q: Why factor the build logic into `reset()` instead of inlining it in the constructor?
options: So calling `reset()` later restores the deck without re-instantiating
Constructor code can't reference `this.cards` until super() runs
Reset() is implicitly called on garbage collection, the constructor isn't
questions.explain: The constructor is just `this.reset()`, so the build logic has exactly one home and starting a new hand costs one call instead of a fresh `new Deck()`. Inlining it in the constructor would force you to duplicate the loop in `reset` or throw the object away between rounds.

questions.q: What does `draw()` return when the deck is empty?
questions.explain: `draw()` is a bare `this.cards.pop()` with no emptiness guard, and `pop` on a length-0 array returns `undefined` without throwing. If an empty deck should be an error, that check has to be added — the silent `undefined` is easy to propagate into a downstream `card.rank` crash.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the Deck so size() prints 52 then 51 after one draw.

L3.prompt: Implement Deck with constructor (builds 52 cards rank+suit), size(), draw() (pop), reset(). Without shuffling: log size, draw 3 cards in order, log size, reset, log size.
hints: Build with two nested loops — suits outside, ranks inside.
Store cards as `rank + suit` strings; no per-card class needed.
draw uses pop() so the last-pushed card (K of clubs here) comes off first.
